slides: Pythagorean triples, a shortcut for the Pythagorean theorem when all the sides are whole numbers.

slides.say: Every Pythagorean triple is three whole numbers that fit the theorem, a squared plus b squared equals c squared. The best-known one is three, four and five. Five is the hypotenuse, because the hypotenuse is always the longest side. Three squared plus four squared is nine plus sixteen, which is twenty-five. And five squared is twenty-five too. It works.

Another triple that shows up on the exam is five, twelve and thirteen. Five squared plus twelve squared is twenty-five plus a hundred forty-four, which is a hundred sixty-nine. And thirteen squared is a hundred sixty-nine too. It works too.

This is quite rare. Most pairs of legs don't give a whole hypotenuse. Legs two and five give four plus twenty-five, which is twenty-nine, so the hypotenuse is the root of twenty-nine. Almost any pair gives a root somewhere, in a leg or in the hypotenuse. That's a fine answer, so don't force a whole number.

That's exactly why the exam loves triples. Everything stays whole, with no messy roots. Most of the time, the exam uses these two triples: three, four, five, and five, twelve, thirteen. There are others, like eight, fifteen and seventeen, but they're very rare, so don't bother learning them. If one shows up, the ordinary theorem still works.

A triple is really a ratio of the sides, three to four to five. That means three units, four of the same units, and five of the same units. The unit can be any length, so we can multiply all three sides by the same number, and it still works. If one unit is seven, multiply three, four and five by seven: twenty-one, twenty-eight and thirty-five. It's the same shape, just bigger, so it's also a right triangle.
at: A triple is really a ratio
Multiply three, four and five by seven

slides: In the same way, five, twelve, thirteen times three is fifteen, thirty-six and thirty-nine. We can multiply by two, by four, by ten, and it always works, as long as the same number multiplies all three sides. And the longest side is always the hypotenuse.

slides.say: Why does it work? Multiply every side by some number k. Then every square is multiplied by k squared: nine k squared plus sixteen k squared is twenty-five k squared. So any positive number works, even a half. Half of three, four, five is one and a half, two, and two and a half.

How do we remember them? Three, four, five is easy, three numbers in a row. For five, twelve, thirteen: high five, a dozen, and one more. Give me a high five, that's five. A dozen, like a box of eggs, that's twelve. And one more, thirteen.
One trap. In a right triangle, you see twenty-seven and thirty-six. If both of them are legs, that's three and four, times nine, so the hypotenuse is five times nine, which is forty-five.
at: If both of them are legs

slides.say: But if thirty-six is the hypotenuse, the numbers aren't in the same places as three, four, five, and the triple doesn't fit. So first find the right angle, then match the triple. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
